placeKinds:
Everyday places someone who lives there goes to, mixed across the neighbourhoods, each worth a conversation and no kind twice: a café, a market stall, a fonda or cocina económica, a taquería or street-food stand, a plaza or jardín, a church, a cantina or mezcalería, a practical shop (farmacia, papelería, tienda de la esquina), the bus terminal, and one or two places that are special to this city or where something is happening (a dance in the plaza, a workshop, a dig). No panaderías (Josh, 2026-10-27: "the conversation is poor"). At least one person with something to show: a scholar, a priest, a museum guide, a professor, a journalist, an archaeologist.

Who is where: at a business, someone who works there (the owner fits too). Customers, students and passers-by only in public places, never in a shop with nothing to sell. Every person has a reason to be at their place today (the `here` line). Kinds: one name per kind, lowercase, the same across cities ("café", "market", "bus-terminal", "church", "plaza").

placeStyles.ciudad-de-mexico: The {neighbourhood} quarter of Mexico City as it really looks today, with its own architecture, street trees and everyday street life. Photorealistic city street photography, taken at eye level from a few steps back with nothing blocking the view: crisp detail, true-to-life saturated colour, bright late-morning sun and dappled light; no haze, no pastel wash, no deep dark shadows
placeStyles.guadalajara: Linocut print with bold carved black lines and wood-grain texture, strong contrast, in bright colour. Palette: terracotta, teal, mustard and sky blue
placeStyles.oaxaca: Mexican shadow-box diorama painted as naive folk art: the scene built inside a small open wooden box, with tiny handmade clay and papier-mâché figures and objects, every surface painted in bright saturated colours with careful small details and alebrije patterns, flat perspective, photographed straight on with soft light. Palette: cochineal red, marigold, indigo and turquoise
placeStyles.puebla: Illustration in the style of a hand-painted Talavera tile panel from Puebla: slightly glossy glaze, visible brush marks, a thin decorative tile border. Palette: cobalt blue and white with touches of yellow, ochre and green
placeStyles.san-miguel-de-allende: Mexican mural painting style: flat fresco look, simplified forms, strong rhythmic composition, matte plaster texture. Palette: terracotta, ochre, rose, slate blue and deep green
placeStyles.guanajuato: Mexican modernist easel painting, in the tradition of the painters born in this region: bold simplified forms, solid volumes, rich earth and jewel colours, visible brushwork on canvas. Palette: ochre, terracotta, emerald, cobalt and warm yellow

placeStyles.patzcuaro: Etching with hand-tinted watercolour: fine black etched lines and cross-hatching, with soft washes of colour laid over them, on cream paper. Palette: lake blue, adobe white, roof red and pine green
placeStyles.merida: Watercolour on rough paper with fine ink outlines, light and airy, strong tropical sun. Palette: Mérida’s pastel colonial walls, ochre, rose, pale lime and white
placeStyles.san-cristobal-de-las-casas: Risograph print in several bright inks on off-white paper: sunny yellow, warm red, leaf green, sky blue and indigo, with visible grain, slight misregistration between the inks, flat overlapping shapes and halftone shading. placeRules: No other words anywhere: no dates, no 'HOY', no neighbourhood or city names, no slogans, no prices, no brand names or logos. Contemporary Mexico: today's clothes and objects, everyday life; no sombreros, skulls, rebozos or costumes. Keep the main scene in the centre; nothing important near the edges.
placeStylesNote: Chosen 2026-10-14 by Josh from the style test (content/es-mx/style-test.json). Each place prompt = city style + the place's scene (its imagePrompt) + its name as the only sign + placeRules (scripts/lib/place-prompt.mjs). The five cities added 2026-11-09 (Guanajuato, Veracruz, Pátzcuaro, Mérida, San Cristóbal) have styles proposed by the cloud session from each city's own craft or look, not yet tested: Josh judges one picture per city first. Veracruz's first idea, a silkscreen travel poster, was dropped as touristy (2026-11-09) for the port's hand-painted sign and boat style. Portraits stay in the one Mexican gouache style (Josh: "mexican portraits are great"). Revised the same night (Josh: the more successful Mexican images were Mexico City, San Miguel and Guadalajara, picture-making techniques rather than the scene rendered as a craft object like Oaxaca's diorama and Puebla's tiles): Guanajuato modernist easel painting, Veracruz 35 mm film photography, Pátzcuaro hand-tinted etching, San Cristóbal two-colour risograph; Mérida watercolour unchanged. San Cristóbal's first places looked forbidding (Josh: "it screams 'don't come here'") while its risograph card looked "x10 better than the places": the card had no lettering and a wide scene full of people, the places a signboard and one person at work. Style kept as on the card; places widened and given life, and public places drawn without a sign (noSignKinds). Then colour (Josh: "here is a hint: color"): the approved card came out in full colour although its prompt said two inks; the places obeyed and came out indigo and red only. San Cristóbal's place style now asks for the card's bright inks. The four northern cities added 2026-11-13 (Tijuana, Monterrey, Mazatlán, Zacatecas) have styles proposed by the cloud chat session, each a way of making a picture and none a craft object, by the lesson above: marker-and-ink urban sketch, hard-edged flat-colour painting, oil pastel, coloured pencil on pink-grey paper. Not yet tested: Josh judges one picture per city first (docs/mexico-north-recipe.md).

cityCards.guanajuato: Mexican modernist easel painting, in the tradition of the painters born in this region: bold simplified forms, solid volumes, rich earth and jewel colours, visible brushwork on canvas. Palette: ochre, terracotta, emerald, cobalt and warm yellow. Guanajuato today: houses in every colour stacked up the sides of a narrow ravine, the yellow dome of the basilica and church towers rising among them, the huge stone statue of El Pípila with his torch on the hill above. At the bottom, a city bus comes out of the stone arch of a tunnel under the town; students sit on a long flight of white stone steps; a woman carries shopping bags up a narrow stepped alley. Contemporary Mexico: today's clothes and objects, everyday life; no sombreros, cacti, skulls, rebozos, costumes or straw-hatted vendors, no sunset glow. Keep the main scene in the centre of the picture; nothing important near the top or bottom edges. Absolutely no words or letters anywhere: no title, no banners, no signs; a picture only, not a poster. Square format.

cityCardsNote: City cards for Mexico's five new cities (2026-11-09, Josh: "lets just start with city portraits"), hand-written in each city's proposed place style, following docs/mexico-version.md → Rules every prompt follows and the recurring defaults to avoid; Josh judges each. The first five cities' cards were made by hand and approved 2026-10-12 (docs/mexico-version.md). Made by scripts/generate-images.mjs --type city. The four northern cities' cards (2026-11-13) are written the same way, in each city's proposed style; Tijuana's shows Avenida Revolución and its arch, not the border fence (a card is an invitation; the fence is a place in the city).
noSignKindsNote: Place kinds drawn with no lettering at all, instead of the place's name on a sign (2026-11-09): a signboard over a church door or on a plaza looked odd in the new cities' first pictures. Shops, cafés, fondas, stalls and terminals keep their sign. Applies to pictures drawn from now on. 'beach', 'park' and 'street market' added 2026-11-13 (Mazatlán's Playa Los Pinos and its shrimp sellers on the pavement, Tijuana's Parque Teniente Guerrero).

travel.about: Prompts for the trip map's pictures (scripts/generate-travel-pictures.mjs; docs/mexico-north-recipe.md): candidate maps of the whole country with no cities on them, in several looks for Josh to pick from by eye (his references, 2026-11-11: "just some ideas - no rules"), and one building per city for the departures board. The app draws the city names, the two ends of the trip and the route, so a map must have no cities. One building alone, never a townscape (Napoli's castle on its rock came out as a hill town); alt is the landmark to try if the first drifts. Sketches go to design/trip-map/<folder>/, not to the app.
travel.mapBody: Accurate outline of the country: the long Baja California peninsula, the Pacific coast, the Gulf of Mexico, the narrow Isthmus of Tehuantepec and the Yucatán peninsula. A few small drawings of landscape only: two snow-capped volcanoes in the centre, cactus and agave in the north, jungle and a stepped pyramid in the Yucatán, two sailing boats and a whale at sea. The neighbouring countries in plain pale grey. A simple title banner reading "MÉXICO" at the top, sea names in neat lettering: "Océano Pacífico" and "Golfo de México", a small compass rose, a thin border. No cities, no city names, no dots or stars for towns, no buildings, no people, no food, no other text.
